Subject: Draft — The shed that tried to become a fire

Spent the last two Saturdays fixing up a shed for a buddy. It’s looking great now: lights work, fan’s secure, and nothing smells like it’s auditioning to become a fire.

Before the cleanup, the electrical setup had the kind of confidence you usually only see in a guy who’s watched three YouTube videos and found a roll of tape.

Power came from three orange extension cords daisy-chained out a basement window, across the yard, and under the deck. One splice was wrapped in duct tape. Not electrical tape. Duct tape—the stuff you use when the fix needs to hold until you can get to the hardware store, except apparently the hardware store never happened.

There was a 30-amp breaker feeding 14-gauge wire, an outlet connected with speaker wire, and a regular outlet wearing a GFCI sticker like that counts as a safety feature. The ceiling fan box was held up by one drywall screw. A mouse nest had moved into a junction box. The mice seemed perfectly comfortable with the whole arrangement, which is more than I can say for me.

And inside the panel door, somebody had written: “SHED – DONT TOUCH – RON.”

I opened the panel and the homeowner asked, “Who’s Ron?” Great question. I was hoping the wiring might know.

We trenched 18 inches, ran proper 12/2 UF cable, put in a 20-amp GFCI breaker and real boxes and outlets, and mounted the fan to a proper brace. The payment plan was two pizzas and a case of Yuengling, which is a pretty good deal—especially since the shed is no longer one loose connection away from making the whole block smell like burnt toast.

Jokes aside, this stuff can start fires. Extension cords aren’t a permanent wiring method, a sticker doesn’t make an outlet GFCI, and the breaker has to match the wire it’s protecting. “It works” is not the same as “it’s safe.”

If you need electrical work, call a licensed electrician. Not your buddy’s buddy who watched a video, not the cheapest cash offer from the neighborhood comments, and not whoever has the most confident-looking tool belt. A good electrician will explain what needs doing and why. Your house—and the people in it—are worth getting it done right.

No names, no tags, and no house details. Just a reminder from a guy who’s seen what happens when a shed full of shortcuts gets one more chance to go wrong.
